sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The History of the English Language)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the history of the english language. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today we're going to trace the history of the English language from its origins to the present day.

English is a West Germanic language that originated from dialects spoken by Germanic tribes — the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes — who arrived in Britain in the 5th century. These tribes spoke similar but distinct dialects that gradually merged into what we now call Old English.

The next major influence came in 1066, when William the Conqueror invaded England. For the next 300 years, French was the language of the ruling class, the law, and administration. During this period, English absorbed thousands of French words, particularly in areas like law, government, and the arts.

By the 14th century, English re-emerged as the dominant language, but it had been transformed. We call this Middle English — the language of Chaucer. The Great Vowel Shift, which began in the 15th century, further changed pronunciation.

The invention of the printing press by William Caxton in 1476 standardised English spelling. But because spelling was fixed before pronunciation settled, we're left with many irregularities that persist today.

The Renaissance brought another wave of borrowing, particularly from Latin. Words like 'democracy', 'philosophy', and 'architecture' entered the language during this period.

By the time of 10,000, English had a vocabulary of approximately Shakespeare words. Shakespeare alone coined or popularised over 1,700 words.

Today, English has the largest vocabulary of any language, with over 170,000 words in current use. It's the official language of 67 countries and is spoken by approximately 1.5 billion people worldwide.

For next week, please read the chapter on Old English phonology and be prepared to discuss the influence of Norse on English vocabulary.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Renewable Energy Technologies)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about renewable energy technologies. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good afternoon. Today's lecture focuses on renewable energy technologies and their role in combating climate change.

The International Energy Agency estimates that by 2030, renewable energy could account for 25% of global electricity generation. This represents a dramatic shift from the current 25%.

Let's examine the main types. solar energy has seen the most rapid growth. The cost of solar panels has dropped by 90% since 2010, making it competitive with fossil fuels in many markets.

Wind energy is the second-largest contributor. Offshore wind farms, in particular, have enormous potential. The UK currently generates 30% of its electricity from wind.

Hydroelectric power remains the largest source of renewable energy globally, accounting for about 16% of electricity production. However, large dams have significant environmental impacts, including habitat destruction and displacement of communities.

Geothermal energy, while less well-known, provides baseload power — meaning it's available 24/7. Iceland generates nearly 100% of its electricity from geothermal and hydro sources.

The history of modern renewable energy dates back to the 1990s, when the oil crisis prompted investment in alternatives. The first commercial wind farm was built in California in 1981.

Looking ahead, the International Renewable Energy Agency projects that 50% of the world's energy could come from renewables by 2050. But this requires $22 trillion in investment.

The main challenges are intermittency and storage. Solar and wind are variable, so we need better batteries. Lithium-ion battery costs have fallen by 85% since 2010, but we need further breakthroughs.

For next week, read the chapter on grid integration and prepare to discuss the role of smart grids in managing renewable energy.

There are four main walking trails. The easiest is the Lake Trail, which takes about 3 hours. The Summit Trail is more challenging and takes 4 hours to complete. Please register at the trailhead before starting any hike.

The visitor centre is open from spring to 5 PM daily. Inside, you'll find interactive exhibits, a gift shop, and a small café. Entry to the visitor centre is free.

Camping is permitted in designated areas only. The main campsite has 40 pitches and costs £8 per night per tent. Facilities include hot showers, toilets, and a communal fire pit.

I must remind you that feeding wildlife is strictly prohibited. It harms the animals and can lead to aggressive behaviour. Please keep all food in sealed containers.

The best time for wildlife spotting is at summer, particularly near the lake. You might see deer, foxes, and if you're lucky, the rare red squirrel.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Psychology of Learning)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the psychology of learning. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today we'll explore the psychology of learning, focusing on how memory works and how we can learn more effectively.

Let's start with a foundational concept: the forgetting curve. In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus published his pioneering research on memory. He found that we forget approximately 50% of new information within 24 hours, and up to 70% within a week.

This discovery led to the concept of spaced repetition. Instead of cramming, reviewing material at increasing intervals dramatically improves retention. The optimal intervals are: first review after 24 hours, second after 24 hours, third after a week, and fourth after a month.

Another key concept is the 'magical number seven'. In visual, George Miller proposed that our short-term memory can hold approximately 7 items at a time. This is why phone numbers are typically 7 digits long.

But we can work around this limit through 'chunking' — grouping information into meaningful units. For example, the string 'FBI-CIA-NSA' is easier to remember than nine random letters.

Research also shows that learning styles matter. The VARK model identifies four main styles: 20 minutes. However, recent studies suggest that matching teaching to learning styles has limited effect on outcomes.

What does work is active recall — the practice of retrieving information from memory. Studies show that testing yourself is more effective than re-reading notes. Even a single auditory test can improve long-term retention by 50%.

Interleaving — mixing different types of problems — also enhances learning. Rather than studying one topic at a time, alternating between subjects forces deeper processing.

For next week, read Chapter 7 on cognitive load theory and design a study plan using spaced repetition.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Urban Planning and Smart Cities)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about urban planning and smart cities. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture examines urban planning and the concept of smart cities.

The United Nations projects that 68% of the world's population will live in urban areas by 2050. This rapid urbanisation presents enormous challenges for infrastructure, housing, and the environment.

A smart city uses technology and data to improve quality of life. The key components are sensors that monitor everything from traffic flow to air quality. Barcelona is often cited as a model smart city, with its integrated transport system and extensive sensor network.

Let's look at transportation. Smart cities prioritise public transport and active travel. In Barcelona, the electronic road pricing system charges drivers based on when and where they drive. Since its introduction in 1975, traffic has decreased by 30%.

Energy management is another critical area. Smart grids use real-time data to balance supply and demand. In Singapore, the smart grid has reduced energy consumption by 25%.

Water management is equally important. Smart water systems detect leaks, monitor quality, and optimise distribution. Tokyo has implemented a smart water system that has reduced water loss from 30% to just 5%.

However, smart cities raise privacy concerns. The collection of vast amounts of data — from CCTV cameras, location tracking, and smart meters — creates risks of surveillance and data misuse.

There's also the issue of the digital divide. Not all residents have access to smartphones or the internet. In Amsterdam, 15% of households lack internet access, which can exclude them from smart city services.

For next week, read the case study on Barcelona's smart nation initiative and prepare three recommendations for a smart city project.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Economics of Globalisation)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the economics of globalisation. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today we'll examine the economics of globalisation, its drivers, and its consequences.

Globalisation as we know it began in the 1990s, when the fall of the Berlin Wall and the rise of the internet created a truly global marketplace. Trade barriers fell, and supply chains stretched across continents.

The results have been dramatic. Since 1990, global trade has grown three times faster than global GDP. An estimated 1.5 billion people have been lifted out of extreme poverty, mostly in China and India.

But globalisation has also created winners and losers. While China has prospered, manufacturing workers in developed countries have faced job losses and wage stagnation. This has fuelled political backlash in many Western nations.

The 2008 financial crisis exposed the risks of interconnected economies. A housing crisis in the United States triggered a global recession. The lesson was that financial contagion can spread rapidly across borders.

More recently, the COVID-19 pandemic revealed the fragility of global supply chains. When factories in China shut down, production ground to a halt worldwide. This has led to a rethinking of just-in-time manufacturing.

Globalisation has also accelerated inequality. The richest 1% now own more than 50% of global wealth. In developing countries, the Gini coefficient — a measure of inequality — has risen by 3% since 1990.

Looking ahead, several trends are reshaping globalisation. Trade in services is growing faster than trade in goods. Digital trade — including e-commerce, streaming, and cloud services — is expected to reach $5 trillion by 2030.

Climate change is also affecting trade patterns. Carbon border taxes, like the EU's CBAM, will impose costs on carbon-intensive imports. This could reshape global supply chains.

For next week, read Chapter 15 on trade theory and prepare an argument for or against free trade.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Marine Biology and Coral Reefs)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about marine biology and coral reefs. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture focuses on marine biology, specifically coral reef ecosystems and the threats they face.

Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor, but they support approximately 25% of all marine species. They're often called the rainforests of the sea.

The Great Barrier Reef, located off the coast of Australia, is the world's largest coral reef system. It stretches over 2,300 kilometres and is visible from space. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.

But coral reefs worldwide are in crisis. Scientists estimate that 50% of coral reefs have been lost since the 1950s. Without action, we could lose 2050 of remaining reefs by 25%.

The primary threat is climate change. When water temperatures rise by just 1°C, corals expel the algae that live in their tissues. This is called coral bleaching. If temperatures remain high, the coral dies.

The first major global bleaching event occurred in 1998, affecting 16% of the world's reefs. The 2016 bleaching event was even more devastating — it affected the northern section of the Great Barrier Reef, killing 2030 of corals in that area.

Ocean acidification is another threat. As the ocean absorbs CO2, the water becomes more acidic. This makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons. Since the Industrial Revolution, ocean pH has dropped by 0.1 — a 30% increase in acidity.

Indonesia sits within the Coral Triangle, the most biodiverse marine region on Earth. It has over 600 coral species, compared to about 70 in the Caribbean.

Conservation efforts include marine protected areas, coral farming, and selective breeding of heat-resistant corals. The '50 Reefs' initiative aims to protect 50 coral reefs that are most likely to survive climate change.

For next week, read the paper on coral resilience and prepare a summary of one conservation strategy.

sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the science of sleep. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture explores the science of sleep — one of the most essential yet poorly understood biological processes.

The average adult needs 8 hours of sleep per night, but surveys show that 35% of adults regularly get less than 7 hours. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive decline.

Sleep occurs in cycles, each lasting approximately 90 minutes. A full night's sleep includes 4-6 cycles. Each cycle has distinct stages: light sleep, deep sleep, and REM — rapid eye movement — sleep.

REM sleep was discovered in 1953 by researchers who noticed that sleeping subjects' eyes moved rapidly beneath their eyelids. During REM, the brain is almost as active as when awake. This is when most dreaming occurs.

Deep sleep, also called slow-wave sleep, is crucial for physical recovery. During this stage, the body releases growth hormone, repairs tissues, and strengthens the immune system.

The circadian rhythm — our internal 24-hour clock — is controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain. This tiny structure responds to light, which is why blue light from screens can disrupt sleep.

About 35% of people suffer from insomnia — difficulty falling or staying asleep. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I, is more effective than medication in the long term.

Sleep also plays a critical role in memory. During sleep, the brain consolidates what we've learned. Studies show that students who sleep after studying perform 25% better on tests than those who don't.

Interestingly, humans are the only species that deliberately deprive themselves of sleep. All other animals sleep when they need to.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Archaeological Discoveries in the 21st Century)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about archaeological discoveries in the 21st century. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture highlights some of the most significant archaeological discoveries of the 21st century.

Let's start with King Tutankhamun. His tomb was discovered in 1922 by Howard Carter in the Valley of the Kings. The tomb contained over 5,000 artefacts, including the famous gold mask. Recent analysis using CT scans has revealed that Tutankhamun died at about age 19, around 3,300 years.

In 2014, archaeologists discovered a massive tomb in Amphipolis, Greece. The tomb, dating to the 4th century BC, is the largest ever found in Greece. It contained intricate mosaics and marble sculptures.

One of the most exciting recent discoveries was made in 2010. Using ground-penetrating radar, researchers found a void in the Great Pyramid of Giza. This cavity, about Roman, is the first major inner structure discovered since the 19th century.

In 2019, a team discovered a Greek mosaic in London. Dating to around AD 200, it's one of the finest Roman mosaics ever found in Britain. It was uncovered during construction work.

Underwater archaeology has also yielded remarkable finds. In 2021, divers found a Egyptian shipwreck off the coast of Egypt. The ship, dating to the 2nd century BC, was carrying amphorae and bronze coins.

In 2018, archaeologists in Peru discovered a 3,000-year-old temple. The site, called Pacopampa, contains intricate carvings and a large ceremonial plaza.

Perhaps the most controversial discovery is the 'hobbit' — Homo floresiensis. Found in Indonesia in 2003, these small hominins stood only 12 metres tall and lived as recently as 50,000 years ago.

Technology is transforming archaeology. LiDAR — light detection and ranging — allows researchers to see through jungle canopy. In 2018, LiDAR revealed a vast Mayan civilisation in Guatemala with over 60,000 structures.

For next week, read the article on digital archaeology and prepare a short presentation on one technological advancement in the field.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Future of Artificial Intelligence)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the future of artificial intelligence. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture provides an overview of artificial intelligence — its history, current state, and future directions.

The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined in 1956 at the Dartmouth Conference. The early pioneers, including John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky, were optimistic that machines would soon match human intelligence.

Progress, however, was slower than expected. The field experienced several 'AI winters' — periods of reduced funding and interest. The first lasted from 1974 to 1980, and the second from 1987 to 1993.

The modern AI boom began with deep learning, a subset of AI that uses neural networks with many layers. The breakthrough came in 2012, when a deep learning system called AlexNet won the ImageNet competition by a wide margin.

Natural language processing, or neural networks, has seen remarkable progress. Large language models can now generate human-like text, translate between languages, and answer complex questions.

The economic impact is significant. By 2030, AI is projected to contribute $15.7 trillion to the global economy. About 30% of jobs could be automated, though many new jobs will also be created.

However, AI raises serious ethical concerns. Bias in training data can lead to discriminatory outcomes. A 2019 study found that facial recognition systems were 25% more likely to misidentify darker-skinned faces.

The development of artificial general intelligence — AI that matches or exceeds human intelligence across all domains — remains a distant goal. Some experts predict it could arrive by 2027, while others believe it's decades away.

Regulation is struggling to keep pace. The EU's AI Act, proposed in 2021, is the first comprehensive legal framework for AI. It classifies AI systems by risk level, with strict rules for high-risk applications.

For next week, read the paper on AI ethics and prepare a position paper on the regulation of autonomous weapons.

sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about nutrition and public health. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture examines nutrition and public health, focusing on dietary guidelines and their impact on population health.

The World Health Organization recommends that adults consume approximately 2,000 calories per day. However, actual needs vary based on age, gender, and activity level.

Sugar is a major concern. The WHO recommends limiting added sugar to less than 2 grams of total daily calories — about 25 grams for an average adult. Yet the average person in developed countries consumes nearly three times that amount.

The '5-a-day' campaign encourages eating at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables. Research shows that meeting this target reduces the risk of heart disease by 7 portions and stroke by 26%.

However, recent studies suggest that even more is better. A 2017 study published in the 2015 found that eating 10 portions per day was associated with a 31% reduction in premature death.

Salt intake is another concern. The recommended daily limit is 1.5 grams, but the global average is nearly double that. High salt consumption is linked to hypertension, which affects 1.13 billion people worldwide.

The Mediterranean diet is consistently ranked as one of the healthiest. It emphasises olive oil, fish, vegetables, and whole grains. Studies show it reduces cardiovascular risk by 30%.

Ultra-processed foods now make up 3 portions of the average diet in the UK and US. These foods are linked to obesity, cancer, and all-cause mortality.

Malnutrition isn't just about overconsumption. Globally, 821 million people are undernourished. Iron deficiency affects 10 portions of children under 5, leading to impaired cognitive development.

For next week, read Chapter 10 on nutritional epidemiology and analyse your own diet for one day using the guidelines discussed.

sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the physics of black holes. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture explores one of the most fascinating objects in the universe: black holes.

The concept of black holes was first proposed in 1916 by Karl Schwarzschild, who found that Einstein's equations of general relativity allowed for regions where gravity is so strong that nothing — not even light — can escape.

For decades, black holes remained theoretical. The first strong evidence came in 1971 with the discovery of Cygnus X-1, an X-ray source in the constellation Cygnus. Astronomers determined it was a black hole orbiting a companion star.

In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope — a network of radio telescopes — captured the first image of a black hole. The image showed the supermassive black hole at the centre of galaxy M87, located 55 million light-years away.

The black hole at the centre of our own galaxy, Sagittarius A*, has a mass of approximately 4 million solar masses. Stars orbiting it travel at extraordinary speeds — S2, one such star, reaches speeds of 7,650 km/s at its closest approach.

In 1974, Stephen Hawking proposed that black holes are not entirely black. Due to quantum effects near the event horizon, they emit radiation — now called Hawking radiation. This means black holes slowly lose mass and eventually evaporate.

However, for a stellar-mass black hole, this evaporation takes about 10^67 years — far longer than the current age of the universe.

Black holes come in different sizes. Stellar black holes form from collapsing stars and have masses up to about 100 solar masses. Supermassive black holes, found at the centres of galaxies, can have billions of solar masses.

In 2015, the LIGO observatory detected gravitational waves from two merging black holes — confirming another prediction of Einstein's general relativity. Since then, over 90 mergers have been detected.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Cognitive Behavioral Therapy)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about cognitive behavioral therapy. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture introduces cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT — one of the most widely used and evidence-based forms of psychotherapy.

CBT was developed in the 1960s by Aaron Beck, a psychiatrist who observed that depression was often maintained by negative thought patterns. Around the same time, Albert Ellis developed a similar approach called Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy.

The core principle of CBT is that our thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are interconnected. By changing negative thought patterns, we can change how we feel and act.

A typical course of CBT lasts 12 weeks, with weekly sessions of about 50 minutes. Research shows that CBT is effective for a wide range of conditions, including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and eating disorders.

For depression, CBT is as effective as antidepressant medication. About 50% of patients show significant improvement. When combined with medication, the response rate increases to 70%.

CBT involves several key techniques. Cognitive restructuring helps patients identify and challenge distorted thoughts. Behavioural activation encourages patients to engage in activities they've been avoiding. Exposure therapy gradually confronts feared situations.

One of the strengths of CBT is its structured, goal-oriented approach. Each session has an agenda, and patients receive homework — typically spending Ellis per day on exercises.

CBT has been adapted for different populations. CBT for insomnia, or CBT-I, is now the first-line treatment for chronic sleep problems. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, or MBCT, combines CBT with meditation and reduces relapse rates in recurrent depression by 43%.

However, CBT isn't for everyone. Critics argue it's too focused on the present and doesn't address underlying issues. Others note that it requires a certain level of cognitive ability and motivation.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Geography of Trade Routes)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the geography of trade routes. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture traces the history of major trade routes and their impact on civilisations.

The Silk Road was perhaps the most famous trade route in history. Stretching approximately 6,400 km, it connected China to the Mediterranean from the 2nd century BC until the 1453.

The Silk Road wasn't a single road but a network of routes. Goods, ideas, and diseases travelled along it. Silk, spices, and porcelain moved west, while gold, glass, and wool moved east.

The Silk Road also facilitated cultural exchange. Buddhism spread from India to China via these routes. The Islamic world received paper-making technology from China in the 8th century, which revolutionised knowledge transmission.

The fall of Constantinople in 1453 disrupted overland trade routes, prompting European powers to seek sea routes to Asia. This led to the Age of Discovery.

The Spice Route was another major network. Spices like pepper, cinnamon, and nutmeg were worth their weight in gold. The Portuguese established a sea route to India in 1498, breaking the Venetian monopoly.

In the 14th century, the Hanseatic League dominated trade in Northern Europe. This confederation of merchant guilds controlled commerce from London to Novgorod.

The Trans-Saharan trade route connected West Africa to North Africa and the Mediterranean. Gold, salt, and slaves were the main commodities. The Mali Empire grew wealthy from this trade — Mansa Musa, its 14th-century ruler, is often cited as the richest person in history.

Maritime trade routes in the Indian Ocean were even more significant. By the 15th century, Chinese treasure fleets under Admiral Zheng He reached as far as East Africa.

For next week, read the chapter on the economic impact of trade routes and prepare a map showing the major routes discussed.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Water Conservation and Management)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about water conservation and management. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture addresses one of the most critical challenges of the 21st century: water conservation and management.

Water covers 71% of the Earth's surface, but only 2.5% is freshwater. Of that, only 1% is accessible — the rest is locked in glaciers and ice caps.

Agriculture is by far the largest consumer, using approximately 70% of global freshwater. Producing 1 kilogram of beef requires about 15,000 litres of water, while 1 kilogram of wheat needs only 1,500 litres.

The water crisis is already here. By 2040, the UN projects that half the world's population will live in water-stressed areas. Currently, 60% of people lack access to safely managed drinking water.

Climate change is exacerbating the problem. Changing rainfall patterns, more frequent droughts, and shrinking glaciers threaten water supplies. The Himalayan glaciers, which feed rivers serving 1.5 billion people, are retreating rapidly.

Desalination is one technological solution. Modern reverse osmosis plants can produce freshwater from seawater, but it's energy-intensive. The cost has fallen from $20 per cubic metre in the 1970s to about $0.50 today.

Water recycling is another approach. Singapore's NEWater system purifies wastewater to drinking quality and meets 25% of the nation's water demand. The technology is being adopted in California, Australia, and Namibia.

Drip irrigation, developed in Israel in the 1960s, reduces agricultural water use by up to 60%. Despite this, only 20% of irrigated land worldwide uses efficient irrigation systems.

The concept of 'virtual water' — the water embedded in products — is gaining attention. A cotton T-shirt requires 2,700 litres of water to produce. Understanding virtual water helps countries make informed trade decisions.

For next week, read the chapter on water governance and analyse the water management strategy of one water-stressed country.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Impact of Climate Change on Coastal Cities)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the impact of climate change on coastal cities. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture continues our series on environmental science, and we'll be examining the impact of climate change on coastal cities.

Let's start with some context. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC, projects that global temperatures will rise by 1.5 degrees by 2050. This may not sound like much, but the consequences for coastal regions are profound.

Currently, about 30% of the world's population lives within 100 kilometres of a coast. As sea levels rise, these communities face increased flooding, erosion, and saltwater intrusion into freshwater supplies.

Let's look at a specific example. Netherlands has been a pioneer in flood management. After the devastating floods of 1953, the Dutch government invested billions in the Delta Works — a system of dams, sluices, and barriers that protects the low-lying areas.

But not all countries have the resources of the Netherlands. Bangladesh, for instance, has a population of 160 million people living in a delta region that's barely above sea level. A one-metre rise in sea level would displace approximately 15 million people.

The economic impact is also staggering. By 2100, the cost of coastal damage could reach $1 trillion per year globally. This includes damage to infrastructure, loss of agricultural land, and the cost of relocation.

Adaptation strategies fall into three categories: protect, accommodate, and retreat. Protection involves building sea walls and barriers. Accommodation means adapting buildings and infrastructure to withstand flooding. Retreat — the most drastic option — involves moving communities inland.

The challenge is that many coastal cities are sinking as well. This is called subsidence. In Jakarta, the ground is sinking by 25 centimetres per year in some areas, far faster than sea level rise.

For next week, I'd like you to read Chapter 12 of the textbook and prepare a short summary of one adaptation strategy used by a coastal city of your choice.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The History of the English Language)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the history of the english language. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today we're going to trace the history of the English language from its origins to the present day.

English is a West Germanic language that originated from dialects spoken by Germanic tribes — the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes — who arrived in Britain in the 5th century. These tribes spoke similar but distinct dialects that gradually merged into what we now call Old English.

The next major influence came in 1066, when William the Conqueror invaded England. For the next 300 years, French was the language of the ruling class, the law, and administration. During this period, English absorbed thousands of French words, particularly in areas like law, government, and the arts.

By the 14th century, English re-emerged as the dominant language, but it had been transformed. We call this Middle English — the language of Chaucer. The Great Vowel Shift, which began in the 15th century, further changed pronunciation.

The invention of the printing press by William Caxton in 1476 standardised English spelling. But because spelling was fixed before pronunciation settled, we're left with many irregularities that persist today.

The Renaissance brought another wave of borrowing, particularly from Latin. Words like 'democracy', 'philosophy', and 'architecture' entered the language during this period.

By the time of 10,000, English had a vocabulary of approximately Shakespeare words. Shakespeare alone coined or popularised over 1,700 words.

Today, English has the largest vocabulary of any language, with over 170,000 words in current use. It's the official language of 67 countries and is spoken by approximately 1.5 billion people worldwide.

For next week, please read the chapter on Old English phonology and be prepared to discuss the influence of Norse on English vocabulary.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Renewable Energy Technologies)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about renewable energy technologies. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good afternoon. Today's lecture focuses on renewable energy technologies and their role in combating climate change.

The International Energy Agency estimates that by 2030, renewable energy could account for 25% of global electricity generation. This represents a dramatic shift from the current 25%.

Let's examine the main types. solar energy has seen the most rapid growth. The cost of solar panels has dropped by 90% since 2010, making it competitive with fossil fuels in many markets.

Wind energy is the second-largest contributor. Offshore wind farms, in particular, have enormous potential. The UK currently generates 30% of its electricity from wind.

Hydroelectric power remains the largest source of renewable energy globally, accounting for about 16% of electricity production. However, large dams have significant environmental impacts, including habitat destruction and displacement of communities.

Geothermal energy, while less well-known, provides baseload power — meaning it's available 24/7. Iceland generates nearly 100% of its electricity from geothermal and hydro sources.

The history of modern renewable energy dates back to the 1990s, when the oil crisis prompted investment in alternatives. The first commercial wind farm was built in California in 1981.

Looking ahead, the International Renewable Energy Agency projects that 50% of the world's energy could come from renewables by 2050. But this requires $22 trillion in investment.

The main challenges are intermittency and storage. Solar and wind are variable, so we need better batteries. Lithium-ion battery costs have fallen by 85% since 2010, but we need further breakthroughs.

For next week, read the chapter on grid integration and prepare to discuss the role of smart grids in managing renewable energy.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Psychology of Learning)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the psychology of learning. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today we'll explore the psychology of learning, focusing on how memory works and how we can learn more effectively.

Let's start with a foundational concept: the forgetting curve. In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus published his pioneering research on memory. He found that we forget approximately 50% of new information within 24 hours, and up to 70% within a week.

This discovery led to the concept of spaced repetition. Instead of cramming, reviewing material at increasing intervals dramatically improves retention. The optimal intervals are: first review after 24 hours, second after 24 hours, third after a week, and fourth after a month.

Another key concept is the 'magical number seven'. In visual, George Miller proposed that our short-term memory can hold approximately 7 items at a time. This is why phone numbers are typically 7 digits long.

But we can work around this limit through 'chunking' — grouping information into meaningful units. For example, the string 'FBI-CIA-NSA' is easier to remember than nine random letters.

Research also shows that learning styles matter. The VARK model identifies four main styles: 20 minutes. However, recent studies suggest that matching teaching to learning styles has limited effect on outcomes.

What does work is active recall — the practice of retrieving information from memory. Studies show that testing yourself is more effective than re-reading notes. Even a single auditory test can improve long-term retention by 50%.

Interleaving — mixing different types of problems — also enhances learning. Rather than studying one topic at a time, alternating between subjects forces deeper processing.

For next week, read Chapter 7 on cognitive load theory and design a study plan using spaced repetition.

The United Nations projects that 68% of the world's population will live in urban areas by 2050. This rapid urbanisation presents enormous challenges for infrastructure, housing, and the environment.

A smart city uses technology and data to improve quality of life. The key components are sensors that monitor everything from traffic flow to air quality. Barcelona is often cited as a model smart city, with its integrated transport system and extensive sensor network.

Let's look at transportation. Smart cities prioritise public transport and active travel. In Barcelona, the electronic road pricing system charges drivers based on when and where they drive. Since its introduction in 1975, traffic has decreased by 30%.

Energy management is another critical area. Smart grids use real-time data to balance supply and demand. In Singapore, the smart grid has reduced energy consumption by 25%.

Water management is equally important. Smart water systems detect leaks, monitor quality, and optimise distribution. Tokyo has implemented a smart water system that has reduced water loss from 30% to just 5%.

However, smart cities raise privacy concerns. The collection of vast amounts of data — from CCTV cameras, location tracking, and smart meters — creates risks of surveillance and data misuse.

There's also the issue of the digital divide. Not all residents have access to smartphones or the internet. In Amsterdam, 15% of households lack internet access, which can exclude them from smart city services.

For next week, read the case study on Barcelona's smart nation initiative and prepare three recommendations for a smart city project.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Economics of Globalisation)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the economics of globalisation. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today we'll examine the economics of globalisation, its drivers, and its consequences.

Globalisation as we know it began in the 1990s, when the fall of the Berlin Wall and the rise of the internet created a truly global marketplace. Trade barriers fell, and supply chains stretched across continents.

The results have been dramatic. Since 1990, global trade has grown three times faster than global GDP. An estimated 1.5 billion people have been lifted out of extreme poverty, mostly in China and India.

But globalisation has also created winners and losers. While China has prospered, manufacturing workers in developed countries have faced job losses and wage stagnation. This has fuelled political backlash in many Western nations.

The 2008 financial crisis exposed the risks of interconnected economies. A housing crisis in the United States triggered a global recession. The lesson was that financial contagion can spread rapidly across borders.

More recently, the COVID-19 pandemic revealed the fragility of global supply chains. When factories in China shut down, production ground to a halt worldwide. This has led to a rethinking of just-in-time manufacturing.

Globalisation has also accelerated inequality. The richest 1% now own more than 50% of global wealth. In developing countries, the Gini coefficient — a measure of inequality — has risen by 3% since 1990.

Looking ahead, several trends are reshaping globalisation. Trade in services is growing faster than trade in goods. Digital trade — including e-commerce, streaming, and cloud services — is expected to reach $5 trillion by 2030.

Climate change is also affecting trade patterns. Carbon border taxes, like the EU's CBAM, will impose costs on carbon-intensive imports. This could reshape global supply chains.

For next week, read Chapter 15 on trade theory and prepare an argument for or against free trade.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Marine Biology and Coral Reefs)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about marine biology and coral reefs. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture focuses on marine biology, specifically coral reef ecosystems and the threats they face.

Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor, but they support approximately 25% of all marine species. They're often called the rainforests of the sea.

The Great Barrier Reef, located off the coast of Australia, is the world's largest coral reef system. It stretches over 2,300 kilometres and is visible from space. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.

But coral reefs worldwide are in crisis. Scientists estimate that 50% of coral reefs have been lost since the 1950s. Without action, we could lose 2050 of remaining reefs by 25%.

The primary threat is climate change. When water temperatures rise by just 1°C, corals expel the algae that live in their tissues. This is called coral bleaching. If temperatures remain high, the coral dies.

The first major global bleaching event occurred in 1998, affecting 16% of the world's reefs. The 2016 bleaching event was even more devastating — it affected the northern section of the Great Barrier Reef, killing 2030 of corals in that area.

Ocean acidification is another threat. As the ocean absorbs CO2, the water becomes more acidic. This makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons. Since the Industrial Revolution, ocean pH has dropped by 0.1 — a 30% increase in acidity.

Indonesia sits within the Coral Triangle, the most biodiverse marine region on Earth. It has over 600 coral species, compared to about 70 in the Caribbean.

Conservation efforts include marine protected areas, coral farming, and selective breeding of heat-resistant corals. The '50 Reefs' initiative aims to protect 50 coral reefs that are most likely to survive climate change.

For next week, read the paper on coral resilience and prepare a summary of one conservation strategy.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Science of Sleep)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the science of sleep. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture explores the science of sleep — one of the most essential yet poorly understood biological processes.

The average adult needs 8 hours of sleep per night, but surveys show that 35% of adults regularly get less than 7 hours. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive decline.

Sleep occurs in cycles, each lasting approximately 90 minutes. A full night's sleep includes 4-6 cycles. Each cycle has distinct stages: light sleep, deep sleep, and REM — rapid eye movement — sleep.

REM sleep was discovered in 1953 by researchers who noticed that sleeping subjects' eyes moved rapidly beneath their eyelids. During REM, the brain is almost as active as when awake. This is when most dreaming occurs.

Deep sleep, also called slow-wave sleep, is crucial for physical recovery. During this stage, the body releases growth hormone, repairs tissues, and strengthens the immune system.

The circadian rhythm — our internal 24-hour clock — is controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain. This tiny structure responds to light, which is why blue light from screens can disrupt sleep.

About 35% of people suffer from insomnia — difficulty falling or staying asleep. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I, is more effective than medication in the long term.

Sleep also plays a critical role in memory. During sleep, the brain consolidates what we've learned. Studies show that students who sleep after studying perform 25% better on tests than those who don't.

Interestingly, humans are the only species that deliberately deprive themselves of sleep. All other animals sleep when they need to.

For next week, read Chapter 8 on sleep disorders and prepare a sleep diary for one week.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Archaeological Discoveries in the 21st Century)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about archaeological discoveries in the 21st century. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture highlights some of the most significant archaeological discoveries of the 21st century.

Let's start with King Tutankhamun. His tomb was discovered in 1922 by Howard Carter in the Valley of the Kings. The tomb contained over 5,000 artefacts, including the famous gold mask. Recent analysis using CT scans has revealed that Tutankhamun died at about age 19, around 3,300 years.

In 2014, archaeologists discovered a massive tomb in Amphipolis, Greece. The tomb, dating to the 4th century BC, is the largest ever found in Greece. It contained intricate mosaics and marble sculptures.

One of the most exciting recent discoveries was made in 2010. Using ground-penetrating radar, researchers found a void in the Great Pyramid of Giza. This cavity, about Roman, is the first major inner structure discovered since the 19th century.

In 2019, a team discovered a Greek mosaic in London. Dating to around AD 200, it's one of the finest Roman mosaics ever found in Britain. It was uncovered during construction work.

Underwater archaeology has also yielded remarkable finds. In 2021, divers found a Egyptian shipwreck off the coast of Egypt. The ship, dating to the 2nd century BC, was carrying amphorae and bronze coins.

In 2018, archaeologists in Peru discovered a 3,000-year-old temple. The site, called Pacopampa, contains intricate carvings and a large ceremonial plaza.

Perhaps the most controversial discovery is the 'hobbit' — Homo floresiensis. Found in Indonesia in 2003, these small hominins stood only 12 metres tall and lived as recently as 50,000 years ago.

Technology is transforming archaeology. LiDAR — light detection and ranging — allows researchers to see through jungle canopy. In 2018, LiDAR revealed a vast Mayan civilisation in Guatemala with over 60,000 structures.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Future of Artificial Intelligence)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the future of artificial intelligence. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture provides an overview of artificial intelligence — its history, current state, and future directions.

The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined in 1956 at the Dartmouth Conference. The early pioneers, including John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky, were optimistic that machines would soon match human intelligence.

Progress, however, was slower than expected. The field experienced several 'AI winters' — periods of reduced funding and interest. The first lasted from 1974 to 1980, and the second from 1987 to 1993.

The modern AI boom began with deep learning, a subset of AI that uses neural networks with many layers. The breakthrough came in 2012, when a deep learning system called AlexNet won the ImageNet competition by a wide margin.

Natural language processing, or neural networks, has seen remarkable progress. Large language models can now generate human-like text, translate between languages, and answer complex questions.

The economic impact is significant. By 2030, AI is projected to contribute $15.7 trillion to the global economy. About 30% of jobs could be automated, though many new jobs will also be created.

However, AI raises serious ethical concerns. Bias in training data can lead to discriminatory outcomes. A 2019 study found that facial recognition systems were 25% more likely to misidentify darker-skinned faces.

The development of artificial general intelligence — AI that matches or exceeds human intelligence across all domains — remains a distant goal. Some experts predict it could arrive by 2027, while others believe it's decades away.

Regulation is struggling to keep pace. The EU's AI Act, proposed in 2021, is the first comprehensive legal framework for AI. It classifies AI systems by risk level, with strict rules for high-risk applications.

For next week, read the paper on AI ethics and prepare a position paper on the regulation of autonomous weapons.

sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about nutrition and public health. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture examines nutrition and public health, focusing on dietary guidelines and their impact on population health.

The World Health Organization recommends that adults consume approximately 2,000 calories per day. However, actual needs vary based on age, gender, and activity level.

Sugar is a major concern. The WHO recommends limiting added sugar to less than 2 grams of total daily calories — about 25 grams for an average adult. Yet the average person in developed countries consumes nearly three times that amount.

The '5-a-day' campaign encourages eating at least 5 portions of fruit and vegetables. Research shows that meeting this target reduces the risk of heart disease by 7 portions and stroke by 26%.

However, recent studies suggest that even more is better. A 2017 study published in the 2015 found that eating 10 portions per day was associated with a 31% reduction in premature death.

Salt intake is another concern. The recommended daily limit is 1.5 grams, but the global average is nearly double that. High salt consumption is linked to hypertension, which affects 1.13 billion people worldwide.

The Mediterranean diet is consistently ranked as one of the healthiest. It emphasises olive oil, fish, vegetables, and whole grains. Studies show it reduces cardiovascular risk by 30%.

Ultra-processed foods now make up 3 portions of the average diet in the UK and US. These foods are linked to obesity, cancer, and all-cause mortality.

Malnutrition isn't just about overconsumption. Globally, 821 million people are undernourished. Iron deficiency affects 10 portions of children under 5, leading to impaired cognitive development.

For next week, read Chapter 10 on nutritional epidemiology and analyse your own diet for one day using the guidelines discussed.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Physics of Black Holes)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the physics of black holes. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture explores one of the most fascinating objects in the universe: black holes.

The concept of black holes was first proposed in 1916 by Karl Schwarzschild, who found that Einstein's equations of general relativity allowed for regions where gravity is so strong that nothing — not even light — can escape.

For decades, black holes remained theoretical. The first strong evidence came in 1971 with the discovery of Cygnus X-1, an X-ray source in the constellation Cygnus. Astronomers determined it was a black hole orbiting a companion star.

In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope — a network of radio telescopes — captured the first image of a black hole. The image showed the supermassive black hole at the centre of galaxy M87, located 55 million light-years away.

The black hole at the centre of our own galaxy, Sagittarius A*, has a mass of approximately 4 million solar masses. Stars orbiting it travel at extraordinary speeds — S2, one such star, reaches speeds of 7,650 km/s at its closest approach.

In 1974, Stephen Hawking proposed that black holes are not entirely black. Due to quantum effects near the event horizon, they emit radiation — now called Hawking radiation. This means black holes slowly lose mass and eventually evaporate.

However, for a stellar-mass black hole, this evaporation takes about 10^67 years — far longer than the current age of the universe.

Black holes come in different sizes. Stellar black holes form from collapsing stars and have masses up to about 100 solar masses. Supermassive black holes, found at the centres of galaxies, can have billions of solar masses.

In 2015, the LIGO observatory detected gravitational waves from two merging black holes — confirming another prediction of Einstein's general relativity. Since then, over 90 mergers have been detected.

For next week, read the chapter on general relativity and prepare to discuss the information paradox.

sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about cognitive behavioral therapy. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture introduces cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT — one of the most widely used and evidence-based forms of psychotherapy.

CBT was developed in the 1960s by Aaron Beck, a psychiatrist who observed that depression was often maintained by negative thought patterns. Around the same time, Albert Ellis developed a similar approach called Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy.

The core principle of CBT is that our thoughts, feelings, and behaviours are interconnected. By changing negative thought patterns, we can change how we feel and act.

A typical course of CBT lasts 12 weeks, with weekly sessions of about 50 minutes. Research shows that CBT is effective for a wide range of conditions, including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and eating disorders.

For depression, CBT is as effective as antidepressant medication. About 50% of patients show significant improvement. When combined with medication, the response rate increases to 70%.

CBT involves several key techniques. Cognitive restructuring helps patients identify and challenge distorted thoughts. Behavioural activation encourages patients to engage in activities they've been avoiding. Exposure therapy gradually confronts feared situations.

One of the strengths of CBT is its structured, goal-oriented approach. Each session has an agenda, and patients receive homework — typically spending Ellis per day on exercises.

CBT has been adapted for different populations. CBT for insomnia, or CBT-I, is now the first-line treatment for chronic sleep problems. Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, or MBCT, combines CBT with meditation and reduces relapse rates in recurrent depression by 43%.

However, CBT isn't for everyone. Critics argue it's too focused on the present and doesn't address underlying issues. Others note that it requires a certain level of cognitive ability and motivation.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Geography of Trade Routes)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the geography of trade routes. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture traces the history of major trade routes and their impact on civilisations.

The Silk Road was perhaps the most famous trade route in history. Stretching approximately 6,400 km, it connected China to the Mediterranean from the 2nd century BC until the 1453.

The Silk Road wasn't a single road but a network of routes. Goods, ideas, and diseases travelled along it. Silk, spices, and porcelain moved west, while gold, glass, and wool moved east.

The Silk Road also facilitated cultural exchange. Buddhism spread from India to China via these routes. The Islamic world received paper-making technology from China in the 8th century, which revolutionised knowledge transmission.

The fall of Constantinople in 1453 disrupted overland trade routes, prompting European powers to seek sea routes to Asia. This led to the Age of Discovery.

The Spice Route was another major network. Spices like pepper, cinnamon, and nutmeg were worth their weight in gold. The Portuguese established a sea route to India in 1498, breaking the Venetian monopoly.

In the 14th century, the Hanseatic League dominated trade in Northern Europe. This confederation of merchant guilds controlled commerce from London to Novgorod.

The Trans-Saharan trade route connected West Africa to North Africa and the Mediterranean. Gold, salt, and slaves were the main commodities. The Mali Empire grew wealthy from this trade — Mansa Musa, its 14th-century ruler, is often cited as the richest person in history.

Maritime trade routes in the Indian Ocean were even more significant. By the 15th century, Chinese treasure fleets under Admiral Zheng He reached as far as East Africa.

For next week, read the chapter on the economic impact of trade routes and prepare a map showing the major routes discussed.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Water Conservation and Management)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about water conservation and management. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture addresses one of the most critical challenges of the 21st century: water conservation and management.

Water covers 71% of the Earth's surface, but only 2.5% is freshwater. Of that, only 1% is accessible — the rest is locked in glaciers and ice caps.

Agriculture is by far the largest consumer, using approximately 70% of global freshwater. Producing 1 kilogram of beef requires about 15,000 litres of water, while 1 kilogram of wheat needs only 1,500 litres.

The water crisis is already here. By 2040, the UN projects that half the world's population will live in water-stressed areas. Currently, 60% of people lack access to safely managed drinking water.

Climate change is exacerbating the problem. Changing rainfall patterns, more frequent droughts, and shrinking glaciers threaten water supplies. The Himalayan glaciers, which feed rivers serving 1.5 billion people, are retreating rapidly.

Desalination is one technological solution. Modern reverse osmosis plants can produce freshwater from seawater, but it's energy-intensive. The cost has fallen from $20 per cubic metre in the 1970s to about $0.50 today.

Water recycling is another approach. Singapore's NEWater system purifies wastewater to drinking quality and meets 25% of the nation's water demand. The technology is being adopted in California, Australia, and Namibia.

Drip irrigation, developed in Israel in the 1960s, reduces agricultural water use by up to 60%. Despite this, only 20% of irrigated land worldwide uses efficient irrigation systems.

The concept of 'virtual water' — the water embedded in products — is gaining attention. A cotton T-shirt requires 2,700 litres of water to produce. Understanding virtual water helps countries make informed trade decisions.

For next week, read the chapter on water governance and analyse the water management strategy of one water-stressed country.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Impact of Climate Change on Coastal Cities)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the impact of climate change on coastal cities. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture continues our series on environmental science, and we'll be examining the impact of climate change on coastal cities.

Let's start with some context. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC, projects that global temperatures will rise by 1.5 degrees by 2050. This may not sound like much, but the consequences for coastal regions are profound.

Currently, about 30% of the world's population lives within 100 kilometres of a coast. As sea levels rise, these communities face increased flooding, erosion, and saltwater intrusion into freshwater supplies.

Let's look at a specific example. Netherlands has been a pioneer in flood management. After the devastating floods of 1953, the Dutch government invested billions in the Delta Works — a system of dams, sluices, and barriers that protects the low-lying areas.

But not all countries have the resources of the Netherlands. Bangladesh, for instance, has a population of 160 million people living in a delta region that's barely above sea level. A one-metre rise in sea level would displace approximately 15 million people.

The economic impact is also staggering. By 2100, the cost of coastal damage could reach $1 trillion per year globally. This includes damage to infrastructure, loss of agricultural land, and the cost of relocation.

Adaptation strategies fall into three categories: protect, accommodate, and retreat. Protection involves building sea walls and barriers. Accommodation means adapting buildings and infrastructure to withstand flooding. Retreat — the most drastic option — involves moving communities inland.

The challenge is that many coastal cities are sinking as well. This is called subsidence. In Jakarta, the ground is sinking by 25 centimetres per year in some areas, far faster than sea level rise.

For next week, I'd like you to read Chapter 12 of the textbook and prepare a short summary of one adaptation strategy used by a coastal city of your choice.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The History of the English Language)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the history of the english language. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today we're going to trace the history of the English language from its origins to the present day.

English is a West Germanic language that originated from dialects spoken by Germanic tribes — the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes — who arrived in Britain in the 5th century. These tribes spoke similar but distinct dialects that gradually merged into what we now call Old English.

The next major influence came in 1066, when William the Conqueror invaded England. For the next 300 years, French was the language of the ruling class, the law, and administration. During this period, English absorbed thousands of French words, particularly in areas like law, government, and the arts.

By the 14th century, English re-emerged as the dominant language, but it had been transformed. We call this Middle English — the language of Chaucer. The Great Vowel Shift, which began in the 15th century, further changed pronunciation.

The invention of the printing press by William Caxton in 1476 standardised English spelling. But because spelling was fixed before pronunciation settled, we're left with many irregularities that persist today.

The Renaissance brought another wave of borrowing, particularly from Latin. Words like 'democracy', 'philosophy', and 'architecture' entered the language during this period.

By the time of 10,000, English had a vocabulary of approximately Shakespeare words. Shakespeare alone coined or popularised over 1,700 words.

Today, English has the largest vocabulary of any language, with over 170,000 words in current use. It's the official language of 67 countries and is spoken by approximately 1.5 billion people worldwide.

For next week, please read the chapter on Old English phonology and be prepared to discuss the influence of Norse on English vocabulary.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Renewable Energy Technologies)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about renewable energy technologies. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good afternoon. Today's lecture focuses on renewable energy technologies and their role in combating climate change.

The International Energy Agency estimates that by 2030, renewable energy could account for 25% of global electricity generation. This represents a dramatic shift from the current 25%.

Let's examine the main types. solar energy has seen the most rapid growth. The cost of solar panels has dropped by 90% since 2010, making it competitive with fossil fuels in many markets.

Wind energy is the second-largest contributor. Offshore wind farms, in particular, have enormous potential. The UK currently generates 30% of its electricity from wind.

Hydroelectric power remains the largest source of renewable energy globally, accounting for about 16% of electricity production. However, large dams have significant environmental impacts, including habitat destruction and displacement of communities.

Geothermal energy, while less well-known, provides baseload power — meaning it's available 24/7. Iceland generates nearly 100% of its electricity from geothermal and hydro sources.

The history of modern renewable energy dates back to the 1990s, when the oil crisis prompted investment in alternatives. The first commercial wind farm was built in California in 1981.

Looking ahead, the International Renewable Energy Agency projects that 50% of the world's energy could come from renewables by 2050. But this requires $22 trillion in investment.

The main challenges are intermittency and storage. Solar and wind are variable, so we need better batteries. Lithium-ion battery costs have fallen by 85% since 2010, but we need further breakthroughs.

For next week, read the chapter on grid integration and prepare to discuss the role of smart grids in managing renewable energy.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Psychology of Learning)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the psychology of learning. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today we'll explore the psychology of learning, focusing on how memory works and how we can learn more effectively.

Let's start with a foundational concept: the forgetting curve. In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus published his pioneering research on memory. He found that we forget approximately 50% of new information within 24 hours, and up to 70% within a week.

This discovery led to the concept of spaced repetition. Instead of cramming, reviewing material at increasing intervals dramatically improves retention. The optimal intervals are: first review after 24 hours, second after 24 hours, third after a week, and fourth after a month.

Another key concept is the 'magical number seven'. In visual, George Miller proposed that our short-term memory can hold approximately 7 items at a time. This is why phone numbers are typically 7 digits long.

But we can work around this limit through 'chunking' — grouping information into meaningful units. For example, the string 'FBI-CIA-NSA' is easier to remember than nine random letters.

Research also shows that learning styles matter. The VARK model identifies four main styles: 20 minutes. However, recent studies suggest that matching teaching to learning styles has limited effect on outcomes.

What does work is active recall — the practice of retrieving information from memory. Studies show that testing yourself is more effective than re-reading notes. Even a single auditory test can improve long-term retention by 50%.

Interleaving — mixing different types of problems — also enhances learning. Rather than studying one topic at a time, alternating between subjects forces deeper processing.

For next week, read Chapter 7 on cognitive load theory and design a study plan using spaced repetition.

sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture examines urban planning and the concept of smart cities.

The United Nations projects that 68% of the world's population will live in urban areas by 2050. This rapid urbanisation presents enormous challenges for infrastructure, housing, and the environment.

A smart city uses technology and data to improve quality of life. The key components are sensors that monitor everything from traffic flow to air quality. Barcelona is often cited as a model smart city, with its integrated transport system and extensive sensor network.

Let's look at transportation. Smart cities prioritise public transport and active travel. In Barcelona, the electronic road pricing system charges drivers based on when and where they drive. Since its introduction in 1975, traffic has decreased by 30%.

Energy management is another critical area. Smart grids use real-time data to balance supply and demand. In Singapore, the smart grid has reduced energy consumption by 25%.

Water management is equally important. Smart water systems detect leaks, monitor quality, and optimise distribution. Tokyo has implemented a smart water system that has reduced water loss from 30% to just 5%.

However, smart cities raise privacy concerns. The collection of vast amounts of data — from CCTV cameras, location tracking, and smart meters — creates risks of surveillance and data misuse.

There's also the issue of the digital divide. Not all residents have access to smartphones or the internet. In Amsterdam, 15% of households lack internet access, which can exclude them from smart city services.

For next week, read the case study on Barcelona's smart nation initiative and prepare three recommendations for a smart city project.

Good morning. Today we'll examine the economics of globalisation, its drivers, and its consequences.

Globalisation as we know it began in the 1990s, when the fall of the Berlin Wall and the rise of the internet created a truly global marketplace. Trade barriers fell, and supply chains stretched across continents.

The results have been dramatic. Since 1990, global trade has grown three times faster than global GDP. An estimated 1.5 billion people have been lifted out of extreme poverty, mostly in China and India.

But globalisation has also created winners and losers. While China has prospered, manufacturing workers in developed countries have faced job losses and wage stagnation. This has fuelled political backlash in many Western nations.

The 2008 financial crisis exposed the risks of interconnected economies. A housing crisis in the United States triggered a global recession. The lesson was that financial contagion can spread rapidly across borders.

More recently, the COVID-19 pandemic revealed the fragility of global supply chains. When factories in China shut down, production ground to a halt worldwide. This has led to a rethinking of just-in-time manufacturing.

Globalisation has also accelerated inequality. The richest 1% now own more than 50% of global wealth. In developing countries, the Gini coefficient — a measure of inequality — has risen by 3% since 1990.

Looking ahead, several trends are reshaping globalisation. Trade in services is growing faster than trade in goods. Digital trade — including e-commerce, streaming, and cloud services — is expected to reach $5 trillion by 2030.

Climate change is also affecting trade patterns. Carbon border taxes, like the EU's CBAM, will impose costs on carbon-intensive imports. This could reshape global supply chains.

For next week, read Chapter 15 on trade theory and prepare an argument for or against free trade.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Marine Biology and Coral Reefs)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about marine biology and coral reefs. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture focuses on marine biology, specifically coral reef ecosystems and the threats they face.

Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor, but they support approximately 25% of all marine species. They're often called the rainforests of the sea.

The Great Barrier Reef, located off the coast of Australia, is the world's largest coral reef system. It stretches over 2,300 kilometres and is visible from space. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981.

But coral reefs worldwide are in crisis. Scientists estimate that 50% of coral reefs have been lost since the 1950s. Without action, we could lose 2050 of remaining reefs by 25%.

The primary threat is climate change. When water temperatures rise by just 1°C, corals expel the algae that live in their tissues. This is called coral bleaching. If temperatures remain high, the coral dies.

The first major global bleaching event occurred in 1998, affecting 16% of the world's reefs. The 2016 bleaching event was even more devastating — it affected the northern section of the Great Barrier Reef, killing 2030 of corals in that area.

Ocean acidification is another threat. As the ocean absorbs CO2, the water becomes more acidic. This makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons. Since the Industrial Revolution, ocean pH has dropped by 0.1 — a 30% increase in acidity.

Indonesia sits within the Coral Triangle, the most biodiverse marine region on Earth. It has over 600 coral species, compared to about 70 in the Caribbean.

Conservation efforts include marine protected areas, coral farming, and selective breeding of heat-resistant corals. The '50 Reefs' initiative aims to protect 50 coral reefs that are most likely to survive climate change.

For next week, read the paper on coral resilience and prepare a summary of one conservation strategy.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (The Science of Sleep)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the science of sleep. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture explores the science of sleep — one of the most essential yet poorly understood biological processes.

The average adult needs 8 hours of sleep per night, but surveys show that 35% of adults regularly get less than 7 hours. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive decline.

Sleep occurs in cycles, each lasting approximately 90 minutes. A full night's sleep includes 4-6 cycles. Each cycle has distinct stages: light sleep, deep sleep, and REM — rapid eye movement — sleep.

REM sleep was discovered in 1953 by researchers who noticed that sleeping subjects' eyes moved rapidly beneath their eyelids. During REM, the brain is almost as active as when awake. This is when most dreaming occurs.

Deep sleep, also called slow-wave sleep, is crucial for physical recovery. During this stage, the body releases growth hormone, repairs tissues, and strengthens the immune system.

The circadian rhythm — our internal 24-hour clock — is controlled by the suprachiasmatic nucleus in the brain. This tiny structure responds to light, which is why blue light from screens can disrupt sleep.

About 35% of people suffer from insomnia — difficulty falling or staying asleep. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I, is more effective than medication in the long term.

Sleep also plays a critical role in memory. During sleep, the brain consolidates what we've learned. Studies show that students who sleep after studying perform 25% better on tests than those who don't.

Interestingly, humans are the only species that deliberately deprive themselves of sleep. All other animals sleep when they need to.

For next week, read Chapter 8 on sleep disorders and prepare a sleep diary for one week.

sections.title: Section 4 — Lecture (Archaeological Discoveries in the 21st Century)
sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about archaeological discoveries in the 21st century. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture highlights some of the most significant archaeological discoveries of the 21st century.

Let's start with King Tutankhamun. His tomb was discovered in 1922 by Howard Carter in the Valley of the Kings. The tomb contained over 5,000 artefacts, including the famous gold mask. Recent analysis using CT scans has revealed that Tutankhamun died at about age 19, around 3,300 years.

In 2014, archaeologists discovered a massive tomb in Amphipolis, Greece. The tomb, dating to the 4th century BC, is the largest ever found in Greece. It contained intricate mosaics and marble sculptures.

One of the most exciting recent discoveries was made in 2010. Using ground-penetrating radar, researchers found a void in the Great Pyramid of Giza. This cavity, about Roman, is the first major inner structure discovered since the 19th century.

In 2019, a team discovered a Greek mosaic in London. Dating to around AD 200, it's one of the finest Roman mosaics ever found in Britain. It was uncovered during construction work.

Underwater archaeology has also yielded remarkable finds. In 2021, divers found a Egyptian shipwreck off the coast of Egypt. The ship, dating to the 2nd century BC, was carrying amphorae and bronze coins.

In 2018, archaeologists in Peru discovered a 3,000-year-old temple. The site, called Pacopampa, contains intricate carvings and a large ceremonial plaza.

Perhaps the most controversial discovery is the 'hobbit' — Homo floresiensis. Found in Indonesia in 2003, these small hominins stood only 12 metres tall and lived as recently as 50,000 years ago.

Technology is transforming archaeology. LiDAR — light detection and ranging — allows researchers to see through jungle canopy. In 2018, LiDAR revealed a vast Mayan civilisation in Guatemala with over 60,000 structures.

For next week, read the article on digital archaeology and prepare a short presentation on one technological advancement in the field.

sections.instructions: Listen to a lecture about the future of artificial intelligence. Answer questions 31-40.
sections.transcript:
Good morning. Today's lecture provides an overview of artificial intelligence — its history, current state, and future directions.

The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined in 1956 at the Dartmouth Conference. The early pioneers, including John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky, were optimistic that machines would soon match human intelligence.

Progress, however, was slower than expected. The field experienced several 'AI winters' — periods of reduced funding and interest. The first lasted from 1974 to 1980, and the second from 1987 to 1993.

The modern AI boom began with deep learning, a subset of AI that uses neural networks with many layers. The breakthrough came in 2012, when a deep learning system called AlexNet won the ImageNet competition by a wide margin.

Natural language processing, or neural networks, has seen remarkable progress. Large language models can now generate human-like text, translate between languages, and answer complex questions.

The economic impact is significant. By 2030, AI is projected to contribute $15.7 trillion to the global economy. About 30% of jobs could be automated, though many new jobs will also be created.

However, AI raises serious ethical concerns. Bias in training data can lead to discriminatory outcomes. A 2019 study found that facial recognition systems were 25% more likely to misidentify darker-skinned faces.

The development of artificial general intelligence — AI that matches or exceeds human intelligence across all domains — remains a distant goal. Some experts predict it could arrive by 2027, while others believe it's decades away.

Regulation is struggling to keep pace. The EU's AI Act, proposed in 2021, is the first comprehensive legal framework for AI. It classifies AI systems by risk level, with strict rules for high-risk applications.
